title: Let the children come (Mark 10:13–16)
hook: the disciples shoo away children, and he's indignant

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard question about divorce, answered from the beginning. Your line was what god joined. Which bond did you strengthen? Day two hundred one.

If you've ever taken a small child somewhere important, you know the look. The one from the person at the desk who's hoping you'll keep the little one quiet and out of the way. Now it's the disciples wearing that look. Parents are bringing their little children to Jesus, just so he'll touch them, lay a hand on their heads. And the disciples step in and send them off. He's busy. He's important. There's a serious conversation going on about divorce and the Law. Take the kids home. And Mark tells us something he tells us nowhere else. When Jesus saw it, he was angry. Not with the parents. Not with the children. With his friends.
screen: `PARENTS BRING THEIR LITTLE ONES.` → `THE DISCIPLES SEND THEM OFF.` → `AND HE'S ANGRY.`

segments.voice: The King James says he was much displeased. The Greek word is stronger: indignant, properly annoyed. Matthew and Luke tell this story too, and both leave that part out. Mark keeps it. Then come the words: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer, in 1611 English, meant allow. Let them come. Don't stop them. And then the line that turns it into a lesson for the grown-ups: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will not enter it. How does a little child receive something? Watch a toddler handed a cookie. There's no negotiating, no asking what's the catch, no working out whether they've earned it. Hands open, and it's theirs. Children then had no standing and nothing to trade. That's the point. The kingdom isn't a prize for the deserving. It's a gift for people who know how to receive one. Mark ends the scene with three verbs: he took them up in his arms, put his hands on them, and blessed them. Not a pat on the head from a distance. Churches read this passage in different settings. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and many Reformed churches baptize infants, and this is one of the passages they often read at a baptism. Baptist and many other churches baptize those old enough to profess faith, and often read it when parents bring a baby to be dedicated and blessed. Either way, the children end up in his arms.
screen: `MARK ALONE SAYS HE WAS ANGRY.` · `SUFFER MEANS ALLOW.` · `RECEIVE IT LIKE A CHILD.` · `ARMS, HANDS, BLESSING.` · then, large: `FOR OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive something the way a child would. Settle, and breathe. Notice one thing you've been given today that you didn't earn. The breath you're taking right now. Sunlight. A message from someone. Your own hands. Don't analyze it. Don't ask whether you deserve it. Just take it, the way a toddler takes a cookie, with open hands. If you pray, you can simply say thank you, like a child would. The bell holds the time.
Let the children come. His angry defense of the little ones, and his lesson: receive the kingdom as a child receives a gift.
Your line: like a child. Today, when someone gives you something, a compliment, help, a gift, don't deflect it. Just say thank you. Day two hundred one.

howItsDone: Many churches that baptize infants read this passage at baptisms, and churches that baptize believers often read it at services where parents present a baby for dedication and blessing.

bring the children to the front.

original.note: Greek: a little child, a small one. the word in Mark 10:13–15.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle picture of Jesus liking kids.
what it means: he is angry at his friends for shutting children out, and says the kingdom is received the way a child receives a gift.
what a scholar hears: Mark alone keeps the anger, aganakteō. and suffer is 1611 English for allow.

sources.quoted: Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.

notes: 'Mark tells us something he tells us nowhere else': aganakteō is used of Jesus only here in the Gospels. Confirm.
Matthew 19:13–15 and Luke 18:15–17 omit Jesus's indignation. Confirm.
